title: In re Judge Jennifer Medley
description: Whether Judge Jennifer M. Medley violated the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Louisiana Constitution through false campaign advertisements and unreported campaign expenditures during her judicial election campaign, with the Judiciary Commission arguing she did and Judge Medley arguing her speech was protected and charges were not proven.
plaintiff_argument: The Judiciary Commission argued that Judge Medley violated Canons 7A(9), 7B(1), and 7B(3) of the Code of Judicial Conduct and La. Const. art. V, § 25(C) by making knowingly false statements in campaign ads and failing to report campaign expenditures.
defendant_argument: Judge Medley argued that her campaign speech was protected by the First Amendment, that the 'deadbeat dad' ad was accurate or at least not knowingly false, and that the failure to report expenditures was unintentional, and that the Commission lacked jurisdiction over campaign finance issues.
decision_outcome: The court ordered Judge Jennifer M. Medley to be suspended from office without pay for thirty days and to reimburse the Judiciary Commission $2,747.41 for costs, finding violations for false campaign statements and unreported expenditures (Counts II and IV) but dismissing charges related to the 'scorned woman' ad and the campaign loan (Counts I and III).

title: State v. Davieontray Breax
description: Whether prosecutors may join capital felony charges with other felony charges in an indictment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that capital and non-capital felony charges can be joined because the 'same mode of trial' refers only to the number of jurors and concurrence required, and this distinction no longer exists after recent legal changes.
defendant_argument: The Defendant argued that capital and non-capital felony charges cannot be joined because they are not triable by the 'same mode of trial,' which encompasses more than just jury composition and verdict concurrence, and that long-standing jurisprudence prohibits such joinder.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's decision, quashed the indictment, and remanded the case, ruling that prosecutors are prohibited from joining capital felony charges with other felony charges.

title: Fremin v. Boyd Racing, LLC
description: Whether Act 437, which legalized historical horse racing without requiring voter approval, is constitutional, with plaintiffs arguing it is a new form of gaming requiring voter approval and defendants arguing it is a new technology for an existing form of gaming that does not require voter approval.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that historical horse racing is a new form of gaming not authorized before October 15, 1996, and therefore requires prior voter approval under the Louisiana Constitution, making Act 437 unconstitutional without such approval.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that historical horse racing is not a new form of gaming but rather a new technology for pari-mutuel wagering, which was already authorized by law, and thus does not require local voter approval.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, declaring Act 437 unconstitutional because historical horse racing is a new form of gaming that requires prior local voter approval.

title: Welch v. United Medical Healthwest-New Orleans
description: Whether La. R.S. 29:771(B)(2)(c)(i), which establishes a gross negligence standard for healthcare provider liability during a public health emergency, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Kathleen Welch, argued that the statute is unconstitutional because it violates due process and adequate remedy provisions, is overbroad, leads to absurd consequences, and is a prohibited special law.
defendant_argument: The defendant, United Medical, argued that the statute is constitutional and that Welch's petition failed to state a cause of action because it only alleged ordinary negligence, not gross negligence as required by the statute during a public health emergency.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Welch's motion to declare La. R.S. 29:771(B)(2)(c)(i) unconstitutional, finding the statute to be constitutional.

title: Fisher v. Harter
description: Whether La. R.S. 13:4163, which grants peremptory grounds for continuances to legislators and legislative employees, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that La. R.S. 13:4163 is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers, individual dignity/equal protection, access to courts, and due process by allowing legislators to unilaterally delay court proceedings.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that La. R.S. 13:4163 is constitutional, does not violate separation of powers, and serves a legitimate governmental interest by allowing legislators and staff time to focus on their jobs.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's decision, declared La. R.S. 13:4163 unconstitutional on its face, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether Charles Ray Thompson received ineffective assistance of counsel during his habitual offender sentencing, leading to an unconstitutionally excessive mandatory life sentence.
plaintiff_argument: Thompson's counsel was ineffective for failing to challenge the excessive mandatory life sentence and present mitigating evidence, resulting in an excessive sentence.
defendant_argument: Thompson failed to prove that his counsel's performance prejudiced him, and the sentence was not excessive enough to warrant a downward departure, as he did not demonstrate "exceptional" circumstances.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of post-conviction relief, vacated Mr. Thompson's life sentence, and remanded the case for resentencing to a term of imprisonment that is not unconstitutionally excessive.

title: Watson Memorial Spiritual Temple of Christ v. Korban
description: Whether a money judgment based on inverse condemnation under the Louisiana Constitution can be enforced via a mandamus action, with the plaintiff arguing it is a ministerial duty and the defendant arguing it requires legislative appropriation and is not subject to mandamus.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the damages awarded for inverse condemnation were a just compensation award, and the constitutional duty to pay just compensation for property taken or damaged is a ministerial duty that courts can compel via a writ of mandamus.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Louisiana Constitution prohibits seizure of state assets to satisfy money judgments, which can only be paid from legislatively appropriated funds, and therefore, courts cannot order appropriation of funds through mandamus.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's ruling, holding that the mandamus suit was not barred by res judicata and that payment of a money judgment for inverse condemnation is a ministerial duty enforceable via mandamus, reversing the district court's dismissal.

title: Bienvenu v. Defendant 1
description: Whether the legislature has the authority, consistent with the due process guarantee of the Louisiana constitution, to retroactively revive a prescribed cause of action for sexual abuse of a minor, where the plaintiff argues it is constitutional and the defendant argues it unconstitutionally divests them of a vested property right.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the legislature has the authority to retroactively revive prescribed claims for child sexual abuse, asserting that the defendants' right to claim liberative prescription is not an absolute vested right and the revival provisions are constitutional under due process.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the retroactive application of the statute unconstitutionally divests them of a vested property right to claim the accrued defense of liberative prescription, which is protected by due process.
decision_outcome: The court vacated its original decree, affirmed the district court's judgment that Act 322, as interpreted by Act 386, is constitutional and applies retroactively to revive all causes of action related to sexual abuse of a minor that previously prescribed, and remanded the case.

title: Bienvenu v. Defendant 1
description: Whether the retroactivity provisions of Act 322, as interpreted by Act 386, which revive certain prescribed child sex abuse claims for a limited three-year period, are constitutional under the due process protections of the Louisiana Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the statutory enactment, as amended by the revival provisions, was constitutional and that the right to claim liberative prescription is not a vested right, or if it is, the revival provisions are still constitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the revival provisions are unconstitutional because the right to plead accrued prescription is a vested property right protected by constitutional due process guarantees, which cannot be divested by the legislature.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's judgment, finding that the statutory enactment reviving prescribed claims for child sex abuse was unconstitutional as it violated due process protections by disturbing defendants' vested property rights, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Mellor v. Jefferson Parish
description: Whether a trial court's order for government entities to remit funds collected under an unconstitutional ordinance into the court's registry violates constitutional provisions regarding the seizure of public funds and the separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the trial court's order was proper as they were owed just compensation for unconstitutionally taken property, and the collected funds were not "public funds" subject to seizure under relevant constitutional and statutory provisions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the trial court's order to remit funds violated constitutional and statutory provisions because the collected fines were "public funds" not subject to seizure, and the order unconstitutionally forced an appropriation by government entities, encroaching on legislative power.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's finding that the June 30, 2022 judgment was interlocutory and not final, and that the defendants' appeal was untimely. However, the court vacated the trial court's order requiring the defendants to remit $2,780,232.02 into the court's registry, finding it violated constitutional provisions regarding public funds and separation of powers. The case was remanded for further proceedings.

title: State v. Lee
description: Whether Article 930.10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure violates the state constitution's separation of powers provision by permitting the judicial branch to exercise the governor's exclusive power to pardon a final conviction.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that Article 930.10 unconstitutionally permits courts to grant clemency to criminal defendants, a power exclusively granted to the governor, thus violating the separation of powers.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Article 930.10 is constitutional, does not violate the separation of powers, and does not infringe upon the governor's right to issue clemency, especially in cases with new evidence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's ruling, vacated the amended conviction and sentence, reinstated the original conviction and sentence, and declared Article 930.10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure unconstitutional.

title: Jameson v. Montgomery
description: Whether absolute prosecutorial immunity shields an assistant district attorney and district attorney from civil liability for alleged misconduct during plea and sentencing phases, specifically misrepresenting a victim's sentencing preference and attempting to conceal misconduct.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the assistant district attorney engaged in intentional misrepresentations and fraudulent conduct, violating the victim's constitutional rights, and that the district attorney is vicariously liable. They contend that absolute immunity should not apply to intentional torts or when a minor victim is involved, and that state statutes provide exceptions to immunity for such misconduct.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue they are entitled to absolute prosecutorial immunity for actions taken within the scope of their prosecutorial duties during the judicial phase of a criminal proceeding, even for alleged intentional or malicious conduct, as established by precedent.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' judgments, sustained the exception of no cause of action, and dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the prosecutors are entitled to absolute immunity.

title: State v. Gleason
description: Whether the common law procedural rule of abatement ab initio, which vacates a conviction when a defendant dies during a direct appeal, should be abandoned in Louisiana.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues the abatement ab initio doctrine should be abandoned in favor of an "Alabama Rule" approach, where the conviction is maintained with a notation of the defendant's death, aligning with Louisiana's policy shift towards victims' rights.
defendant_argument: The defense contends that the right to appeal in Louisiana is constitutionally protected, unlike other states, and any change to the abatement ab initio doctrine should be left to the legislature.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeal's ruling, dismissed the appeal, and remanded the matter to the trial court with instructions to note in the record that the conviction removed the defendant's presumption of innocence but was neither affirmed nor reversed due to his death.

title: State v. Allen
description: Whether Kevin O'Brien Allen was denied effective assistance of counsel in relation to his habitual offender sentencing, leading to an unconstitutionally excessive life sentence.
plaintiff_argument: The trial court correctly denied the motion to reconsider the sentence, finding the life sentence was required by statute.
defendant_argument: Kevin O'Brien Allen argued he was denied effective assistance of counsel because his attorney failed to argue the mandatory life sentence was excessive and failed to present mitigating evidence, resulting in an unconstitutionally excessive sentence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's ruling, vacated Mr. Allen's life sentence, and remanded the case for resentencing to a term of imprisonment that is not unconstitutionally excessive.

title: State v. Reddick
description: Whether the new rule announced in Ramos v. Louisiana, requiring unanimous jury verdicts, applies retroactively to cases on state collateral review.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the Ramos rule should not apply retroactively to cases on state collateral review, citing the Teague framework, the Supreme Court's decision in Edwards, and the burden on the justice system.
defendant_argument: Reginald Reddick argues that the Ramos rule should apply retroactively to cases on state collateral review, asserting it is a watershed rule or that the Teague approach should be modified.
decision_outcome: The court held that the new rule of criminal procedure announced in Ramos, which provides for unanimity in jury verdicts, is not retroactive in Louisiana for cases on state collateral review.

title: Westlawn Cemeteries, LLC v. The Louisiana Cemetery Board
description: Whether Louisiana Administrative Code 46:XIII.1503 C, which requires trust income not remitted within 120 days to become part of the trust principal, is unconstitutional because it exceeds the Louisiana Cemetery Board's statutory authority and conflicts with legislative intent, or if it is a constitutional and valid administrative promulgation.
plaintiff_argument: Westlawn argued that LAC 46:XIII.1503 C is unconstitutional because it exceeds the LCB's statutory authority, directly conflicts with La. R.S. 8:454.1, violates substantive due process rights, is void for vagueness, and constitutes an improper exercise of primary legislative authority.
defendant_argument: The LCB argued that LAC 46:XIII.1503 C is constitutional as a valid promulgation pursuant to legislative authority, merely determines facts upon which La. R.S. 8:454.1 C operates, is administrative in nature, and serves to protect perpetual trust income and ensure regular cemetery maintenance.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, finding that the Louisiana Cemetery Board exceeded its authority in promulgating LAC 46:XIII.1503 C, and therefore declared the rule unconstitutional on its face.

title: Mellor v. The Parish of Jefferson
description: Whether the Jefferson Parish ordinance establishing a School Bus Safety Enforcement Program (SBSEP) is constitutional, given its mandate for the School Board to administer the system, which the plaintiffs argue violates constitutional provisions limiting local government authority over school boards, while the defendant argues it is a valid exercise of power consistent with the School Board's duties.
plaintiff_argument: The SBSEP is unconstitutional because it violates Louisiana Constitution Article VI, Section 5(G) and Article VIII, Section 10(A) by mandating the School Board, an independent state entity, to administer the program.
defendant_argument: The SBSEP is constitutional as it is consistent with the School Board's mandates to provide safe student transportation, and the School Board voluntarily agreed to administer it without its enforcement power being impermissibly usurped.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, finding the School Bus Safety Enforcement Program (SBSEP) ordinance unconstitutional and remanded the matter for further proceedings.

title: Calcasieu Parish School Board Sales v. Nelson Industrial Steam Co.
description: Whether Act 3 violates the Tax Limitation Clause by levying a new tax or increasing an existing tax without a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Legislature.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Act 3 was merely interpretative, clarifying existing law, and did not impose a new tax, thus not requiring a supermajority vote.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Act 3 created a new tax by narrowing a tax exclusion, and therefore was unconstitutional because it failed to garner the required two-thirds supermajority vote.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's ruling that Act 3 is unconstitutional because it imposed a new tax without the required supermajority vote, dismissing the plaintiff's claims.

title: Bayou Bridge Pipeline, LLC v. 38.00 Acres
description: Whether an award of attorney fees and other litigation costs to defendant landowners in an expropriation proceeding may be upheld under current law, specifically when the expropriating entity is private and the award is based on the Louisiana Constitution of 1974 rather than statutory law.
plaintiff_argument: BBP argued that statutory law (La. R.S. 13:5111) does not allow for attorney fees in this case because BBP is not a state agency, and that the Louisiana Constitution's 'just compensation' clause does not provide for such awards in expropriation actions.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued they were entitled to attorney fees and litigation costs under statutory law because BBP acted as a government agent, and that the Louisiana Constitution's 'full extent of his loss' provision includes attorney fees and damages for due process violations.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the court of appeal's award of attorney fees and litigation costs to the defendants, finding the basis for the award in the Louisiana Constitution of 1974, and remanded the matter to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Lowther v. Town of Bastrop
description: Whether a writ of mandamus can compel a municipality to satisfy a judgment for back wages owed to its firefighter employees, with the plaintiffs arguing it is a ministerial duty and the defendant arguing it is a discretionary act requiring appropriation.
plaintiff_argument: The Firefighters argued that the City has a statutorily and constitutionally mandated ministerial duty to pay or appropriate funds for their back wages, enforceable by a writ of mandamus.
defendant_argument: The City argued that paying a judgment is a discretionary act requiring appropriation, not a ministerial duty, and thus cannot be compelled by a writ of mandamus.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' decision, finding that the Firefighters' petition for a writ of mandamus stated a valid cause of action.
